common_name: Coral Berry Aechmea (Fulgens Bromeliad, Scarlet-Berried Urn Plant)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container outside zone 10; Aechmea fulgens cannot tolerate temperatures below 45F. Keep the small central cup topped with filtered or rainwater and pot in a coarse bark-based bromeliad mix.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect shade -- Aechmea fulgens tolerates lower light than many bromeliads and holds its color well as a windowsill or shaded porch plant. This compact Brazilian species forms a loose rosette of soft, powdery grey-green leaves and, unlike showier Aechmea relatives, is grown as much for its persistent fruit display as its bloom: a short, upright spike of small violet-tipped flowers on red pedicels matures into a cluster of glossy coral-red berries that remain ornamental for several months. Keep the cup lightly filled with water and avoid heavy fertilizer, which can scorch the fine root system. Pot offsets separately once they reach roughly a third the size of the parent rosette.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Aechmea fulgens culture notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Bromeliads for Florida landscapes

common_name: Caudata Aechmea (Golden Urn Plant, Yellow-Green Tank Bromeliad)

planting.note: Grow outdoors on a shaded patio or porch in zone 10-12, or as a year-round houseplant elsewhere; move containers indoors well before nighttime temperatures approach 45F. Grow in a loose, fast-draining bark mix and keep the central cup topped with water.

directions: Grow in moderate to bright indirect shade; Aechmea caudata handles lower indoor light better than many tank bromeliads while still coloring up nicely under filtered sun. This Brazilian forest-floor species forms a lax, arching rosette of soft yellow-green leaves -- some collector strains show broad cream-white leaf stripes -- around a shallow central tank. An erect, branched flower spike of small yellow petals emerging from yellow-orange bracts appears in warmer months, later giving way to orange-red berries. Divide and repot offsets once they have formed their own roots, and avoid letting the coarse potting mix stay soggy for long stretches.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Aechmea species notes

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or mounted on bark under shade cloth in zone 10-11, or as an indoor plant in cooler climates. Aechmea calyculata dislikes standing in soggy mix, so use an open, chunky bromeliad blend and let it dry slightly between waterings of the small cup.

directions: Grow in filtered shade with good air movement -- this small, clumping species from Brazil, Paraguay, and Argentina naturally colonizes tree branches in fairly bright forest-edge conditions and rewards a bit more light than typical deep-shade bromeliads. Narrow, soft mid-green leaves form dense offsetting clusters, and short-stalked heads of golden-yellow flowers open in late summer and fall just above the foliage, giving a long season of small but abundant color. Because the plant naturally clumps into an epiphytic mat, it is well suited to mounting on driftwood or growing in a shallow, well-drained hanging basket rather than a deep pot. Trim and reset overcrowded offsets every couple of years to keep the clump from smothering itself.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Aechmea species notes

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio accent in zone 10-12; keep well away from any chance of frost. Water the central cup with distilled or rainwater and let the potting mix approach dryness between waterings.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light rather than direct sun, which can bleach the glossy foliage of this Dutch-bred florist hybrid. Guzmania 'Luna' forms a neat rosette of solid green, strap-shaped leaves topped by an upright, torch-like spike of pale chartreuse-yellow bracts that holds its color for several months, making it a popular unscented alternative to the more common orange and red guzmanias sold at retail. Like other guzmanias it flowers only once per rosette before slowly declining, so plan on potting up the basal offsets that form at the plant's base to keep the display going. Keep humidity moderate to high and avoid cold drafts, which can cause the bract color to fade prematurely.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Guzmania hybrid cultivar notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Guzmania for interior plantscapes

planting.note: Grow as an interior plant or shaded lanai accent in zone 10-12. Keep the cup filled with soft water and avoid tap water high in minerals, which can leave crusty deposits on the variegated foliage.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light to bring out the cream-striped variegation without scorching the leaf tips. Guzmania 'Rana' is a Dutch trade hybrid grown for its combination of longitudinally striped green-and-cream foliage and a bold, upright torch of red-orange bracts that lasts for weeks on end, giving it strong shelf appeal as a gift or accent plant. Culture matches other torch guzmanias: keep the central cup topped with water, grow in an airy bark-based mix, and expect the rosette to die back slowly after flowering while offsets take over. Protect from any temperature below 50F, which can cause blotching on the variegated leaves.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Guzmania hybrid cultivar notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Guzmania for interior plantscapes

planting.note: Plant in a large in-ground bed or oversized container in zone 10-11 where its mature size can be accommodated; it needs many years of frost-free growth before it is large enough to flower. Grow in coarse, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter and give it room -- mature rosettes can exceed 6 feet across.

directions: Site in filtered sun to light shade with room to grow into one of the largest bromeliads cultivated outside the genus Puya. Vriesea imperialis is native to rocky, high-elevation forest edges in southeastern Brazil and forms an immense rosette of broad, silvery-green, channeled leaves that can take a decade or more of frost-free growth before the plant is mature enough to bloom. When it finally flowers, a massive, candelabra-like branched spike rises several feet above the foliage, carrying hundreds of yellow-green flowers over many weeks. Because the rosette dies after flowering, allow the large pups that form around the base plenty of space to develop into the next generation, and expect this species to function as a long-term landscape investment rather than a quick-turnaround plant.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Vriesea species notes

planting.note: Grow as a shaded patio or greenhouse specimen in zone 10-12; protect from any temperature near freezing. Pot in a loose bark-based bromeliad mix and keep the central cup filled with water.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect shade under high humidity -- this Brazilian species prefers the diffuse light of a shaded greenhouse or an understory planting rather than direct sun. Vriesea philippocoburgii forms a broad, soft-textured rosette of glossy green leaves and produces a tall, flattened, sword-shaped flower spike marked with alternating bands of yellow-green and maroon, prized among specialty collectors for the bold color pattern of the bracts themselves rather than the small flowers they hold. Keep the tank topped with rainwater or filtered water and avoid letting the coarse growing medium dry out completely, since this species is less drought-tolerant than many of its Vriesea relatives. After the single rosette flowers and slowly declines, pot up the basal offsets to continue the clump.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Vriesea species notes

planting.note: Plant in a shaded to partly sunny bed or large container in zone 10-11; site it where its wide mature spread and sharp-toothed leaves won't crowd a walkway. Grow in a fast-draining, bark-amended mix and keep the central cup filled with water.

directions: Grow in partial sun to light shade to bring out the strongest leaf coloring without risking scorch on this large-growing Brazilian species. Neoregelia carcharodon takes its common name from the heavily hooked, shark-tooth-like spines lining the margins of its broad, leathery leaves, which form an imposing wide rosette well suited to anchoring a shaded bed or large patio container. As with other blushing bromeliads, the inner leaves color deep wine-red to purple just before the small violet flowers open low in the central cup. Give it plenty of room to reach full size and handle it carefully when repotting, since the marginal teeth are sharp enough to catch skin and clothing.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Neoregelia species notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Bromeliads for Florida landscapes

common_name: Tiger Cub Bromeliad (Compact Striped Neoregelia Hybrid)

planting.note: Grow in a small container or terrarium in zone 10-11, or as a windowsill houseplant elsewhere. Keep the tiny central cup lightly filled with water and avoid letting the shallow root zone dry out completely between waterings.

directions: Grow under bright, filtered light to intensify the dark banding on this dwarf hybrid's foliage. Neoregelia 'Tiger Cub' forms a tight, miniature rosette of olive-green leaves marked with irregular dark tiger-like crossbands, and the small central cup flushes bright red-orange as the plant approaches bloom. Its compact size makes it a natural fit for dish gardens, terrariums, or mounted mini-bromeliad displays where full-sized neoregelias would quickly outgrow the space. Divide and pot up offsets as soon as they form roots of their own, since crowded pups can distort the tidy rosette shape that makes this cultivar desirable.

common_name: Absolute Zero Earth Star (Near-Black Cryptanthus Cultivar)

planting.note: Grow as a terrarium or dish-garden plant in zone 10-12, or as a houseplant elsewhere; this terrestrial bromeliad has no water-holding cup, so keep the potting mix evenly moist rather than flooding a central rosette.

directions: Grow under bright, indirect light -- enough intensity brings out the near-black, deep purple-charcoal foliage that gives this cultivar its name, while too little light lets the color fade toward plain green. Cryptanthus 'Absolute Zero' forms a flat, wavy-edged starfish rosette typical of earth stars, spreading slowly by short stolons that produce new plantlets at the base. Because it has no central water tank like tank-forming bromeliads, water by keeping the fine, fibrous root zone lightly moist rather than by filling a cup. Its small size and dramatic color make it a striking accent among lighter-colored cryptanthus and other terrarium plants.

common_name: Banded Billbergia (Vittata Queen's Tears, Striped Urn Plant)

planting.note: Plant in partial shade in well-draining soil or a hanging container in zone 9-11; established clumps handle brief cold snaps better than more tender bromeliads. Divide crowded offsets any time during the growing season.

directions: Grow in partial shade to bright filtered light; Billbergia vittata tolerates a wider light range than most tank bromeliads, coloring up nicely with more sun but still performing well in shadier spots. This Brazilian species forms tall, narrow, tubular rosettes of silvery-grey leaves crossbanded in a darker green, giving the whole plant a distinctive striped appearance even before it flowers. In spring, a pendant flower spike emerges bearing rose-pink bracts and blue-green petaled flowers, similar in form to the more common Billbergia nutans but with bolder banded foliage. Keep the central cup filled with water and let clumps colonize by offsets, dividing only when the container becomes overcrowded.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Billbergia species notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Billbergia for Florida landscapes

planting.note: Plant in partial shade to filtered sun in well-draining soil or a container in zone 9-11; it spreads readily by offsets and naturalizes well under trees. Divide congested clumps every few years to keep them vigorous.

directions: Grow in partial shade to filtered sun; Billbergia amoena is an adaptable Brazilian species that forms loose, spreading colonies of dusty grey-green, tubular leaves in open woodland and coastal scrub in the wild. Its nodding flower spike appears mostly in winter and spring, showing pink to red bracts and slender green petals edged in deep blue, a color combination shared with several of its Billbergia relatives but on a somewhat smaller, more clumping plant. It tolerates brief cold snaps once established outdoors in zone 9, making it a reasonable companion to Billbergia nutans in a cold-hardy bromeliad planting. Keep the small central cup filled with water and allow offsets to fill in naturally rather than dividing too aggressively.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Billbergia species notes

common_name: Muriel Waterman Billbergia (Variegated Queen's Tears Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant offsets in partial shade in well-draining soil or a container in zone 9-11. This heirloom cultivar is propagated only by division, since its variegation does not come true from seed.

directions: Grow in partial shade to bright filtered light to preserve the crisp cream-white leaf stripes without scorching them. Billbergia 'Muriel Waterman' is a long-cultivated variegated selection, valued for pairing the same nodding, pink-bracted, blue-and-green flower spike found on Billbergia nutans with boldly striped foliage that stays ornamental year-round even when the plant isn't in bloom. It shares the easygoing, cold-tolerant nature of its species parent, handling the same range of outdoor conditions in zone 9-11. Divide rooted offsets from the base of the clump to propagate, since variegated bromeliad cultivars like this one must be increased vegetatively to keep their leaf pattern.

common_name: Foster's Silver Dyckia (Sculptural Silver Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets in spring into very well-drained, gritty soil in full sun; established clumps spread by offsets and can be divided at almost any time during the growing season.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty or rocky soil in full sun; this small terrestrial bromeliad from Brazil forms a tight, symmetrical rosette of narrow, intensely silver-white leaves edged with fine recurved spines, the metallic color intensifying under strong light. In spring, wiry flower stalks rise above the foliage carrying small orange blooms that draw pollinators, though the rosette itself remains the main attraction year-round. Like other dyckias it has no central water-holding cup and is a true sun-and-drought lover, so keep it in lean, sharply drained soil rather than rich garden beds where rot becomes the primary risk. It makes an excellent companion to agaves and other small architectural succulents in a rock garden or gravel bed.

common_name: Fireworks Bromeliad (Liboniana Quesnelia, Cascading Torch Bromeliad)

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or mounted on bark in partial shade in zone 9-11; established plants tolerate brief dips into the upper 20sF. Divide rooted offsets from the base to propagate.

directions: Grow in partial shade with good air movement, ideally in a hanging basket or mounted on bark where its pendant flower spikes can hang freely. Quesnelia liboniana is a Brazilian epiphyte that forms an arching rosette of narrow, finely toothed leaves, and its common name comes from the spectacular downward-cascading flower spike of vivid red-orange bracts tipped with electric blue-violet flowers, resembling a burst of fireworks frozen in place. The display lasts for several weeks and is among the most photographed blooms in the Quesnelia genus. Keep the small central cup filled with water, grow in a coarse, well-drained bark mix, and avoid heavy fertilizer, which can weaken the flower color.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Quesnelia species notes

planting.note: Plant outdoors in partial shade to filtered sun in zone 9-11, or grow as a container specimen elsewhere. Divide crowded offsets from the base of the parent rosette to propagate.

directions: Grow in filtered sun to partial shade -- enough light to bring out the mottled leaf pattern this Brazilian species is named for, without the harsh exposure that can bleach it out. Quesnelia marmorata forms a broad, arching rosette of grey-green leaves irregularly marbled and blotched with maroon-purple, making it an attractive foliage plant even outside of bloom. When it does flower, an upright, cone-shaped spike of pink bracts and blue flowers rises from the center of the cup, complementing rather than overshadowing the patterned leaves. Keep the central tank topped with water and grow in a coarse, fast-draining bromeliad or orchid mix; established clumps are tough and long-lived outdoors in frost-free winters.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Quesnelia species notes

common_name: Blushing Bromeliad (Fulgens Nidularium, Orange-Spotted Bird's Nest)

planting.note: Grow as deep-shade groundcover outdoors in zone 10-12, or as a houseplant elsewhere; protect from any temperature below 40F. Grow in a rich but fast-draining bark and leaf-mold mix and keep the central nest lightly filled with water.

directions: Grow in deep, bright-filtered shade -- Nidularium fulgens is native to the darkest understory of Brazil's coastal rainforest and tolerates lower light than almost any other tank bromeliad in cultivation, making it a reliable groundcover beneath dense tree canopy. Apple-green leaves flecked with darker green spots form a broad rosette, and as bloom time approaches the inner leaves flush brilliant red, creating a nest-like collar around the small white flowers marked in violet-purple that open low in the cup. Because the plant naturally spreads into loose colonies by offsets, it works well massed as a shaded landscape groundcover in addition to container culture. Keep the growing medium consistently moist but never waterlogged, and mist occasionally in dry indoor air to mimic its humid native habitat.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Nidularium species notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Bromeliads for Florida landscapes

planting.note: Plant offsets in partial shade to filtered sun in well-draining soil or a container in zone 9-11. Divide crowded colonies by separating rooted offsets from the base.

directions: Grow in filtered sun to partial shade in a well-draining bed or container; this clump-forming Brazilian terrestrial species handles noticeably more light than most tank bromeliads, reflecting its native habitat on rocky, sun-exposed outcrops. Stiff, arching, mid-green rosettes slowly multiply into a dense colony, and when mature, each rosette sends up a striking columnar spike of tightly overlapping bright red bracts held well above the foliage, resembling a small torch. The bloom spike remains colorful for weeks before the flowering rosette declines, by which time the surrounding offsets are usually well established. Keep soil evenly moist during active growth but let it drain freely, since prolonged sogginess is more damaging to this species than an occasional dry spell.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Orthophytum species notes

planting.note: Grow as a deep-shade understory plant outdoors in zone 10-12, or as a houseplant elsewhere; keep well away from temperatures below 45F. Grow in a rich, fast-draining bark mix and keep the central tank topped with water.

directions: Grow in bright to deep filtered shade -- Canistrum lindenii is native to the dim understory of Brazil's Atlantic Forest and is one of the more shade-tolerant tank bromeliads available, thriving where many other flowering species would stall. Broad, glossy, arching leaves form a wide rosette around a central tank, and the plant flowers by pushing up a compact, nest-like cluster of pure white bracts from which violet-blue flowers emerge one at a time over an extended period, giving a long-lasting, low-growing centerpiece bloom. Because it tolerates such low light, it makes an especially good groundcover choice beneath dense tree canopy or in the darker corners of an indoor plant collection. Keep the tank filled with rainwater or filtered water and avoid direct sun, which can quickly scorch the broad leaves.
sources: Bromeliad Society International -- Canistrum species notes
